title: From problem to running program
subtitle: A computer does exactly what it is told, nothing more. Learn to tell it clearly: plan, write, compile, run, fix.

ps.title: Problem solving
ps.body: Programming starts with a precise problem statement: what are the inputs, what output is wanted, and what rule links them? An algorithm is a finite, unambiguous sequence of steps that solves it. Write it first as plain steps (pseudocode) or a flowchart, then translate to code. Good algorithms are correct, finite, and efficient.

flow.title: Flowcharts
flow.body: Ovals start/stop, parallelograms do input/output, rectangles process, diamonds decide. Follow the arrows: this chart finds the larger of two numbers.

pipe.title: Compile, link, run
pipe.body: C source (.c) is turned into a program by stages: the preprocessor expands #include and macros; the compiler translates to machine code in object files (.o) and reports syntax errors; the linker joins object files and libraries into an executable; the loader puts it in memory to run. Errors come in three kinds: syntax (compile time), logic (wrong answer) and runtime (crash).

struct.title: Structure of a C program
struct.body: Every program has main(), where execution starts; statements end with ;; blocks use { }; /* … */ and // are comments. Below, run it and watch each line execute. (The lab runs a C/C++ subset: cout here plays the role of printf.)

types.title: Variables and data types
types.body: A variable is a named memory location with a type that fixes its size and meaning: char (1 byte), int (usually 4), float (4, ≈7 digits), double (8, ≈15 digits). Declare before use; initialise before reading — an uninitialised local holds garbage. Identifiers: letters, digits, underscore; not starting with a digit; case-sensitive.
types.steps: A signed 8-bit char can hold 2⁸ = 256 values. Range is −128 … 127.

const.title: Constants and style
const.body: Use const or #define for fixed values (PI, MAX) instead of “magic numbers”. Choose descriptive names, indent consistently, comment the why. Code is read far more often than it is written.
